Course · Whole course on one page

The ternary machine: from a trit to a running program

Every lesson is something to press. Each widget runs the fn bodies of a t27 spec compiled to WebAssembly, so the trits you see are the spec computing, beside the spec you can open in the player.

Course 8, 27 lessons, a live widget and a t27 spec in each: why three, balanced ternary, three-valued logic, adders, multiplying without a multiplier, trits in binary memory, the TRI-27 instruction word, a ternary machine and ternary neurons. Every number on a widget is computed by a compiled t27 spec.

Every course is free, for everyone: no sign-up, no email, nothing to pay.

01

Module 1 · Three values

Why three, how balanced ternary writes every number without a sign, and what flipping and cutting trits do.

01

Lesson 1 of 27

Why three

You will learnWhy base 3 is the cheapest whole base to write numbers in, and what that argument leaves out.

Writing a number in base b takes some digits, and every digit must tell b states apart. Price a digit at b and a number costs b times its digit count. The widget runs the spec's own cost(): every number up to 999999 costs 39 in base 3 and 40 in bases 2 and 4. Over a long range the price per digit is b / ln b, smallest at e; 3 is the whole base nearest to it. The model leaves out why binary won: two-state parts are cheap, fast and robust.

Try it

Pick each range in turn and note the cheapest base; find the range where base 2 wins, and say why the curve still favours 3.

Open the interactive lesson →
02

Lesson 2 of 27

Balanced ternary

You will learnHow the digits -1, 0 and +1 write every integer, negative ones included, without a sign.

Balanced ternary weighs its places 1, 3, 9, 27 and lets each digit be -1, 0 or +1. Then 8 is 9 - 1 and -8 is -9 + 1: the sign lives in the digits. Six trits reach from -364 to +364, and every number in that range has exactly one form. The tiles under the counter are trit_at() of the spec, called once per place; one of its tests reads every number from -400 to 400 back from its trits.

Try it

Count up from -13 to 13 and watch which tile changes; find the number at which a fourth trit appears.

Open the interactive lesson →
03

Lesson 3 of 27

Flip to negate, cut to round

You will learnWhy negation is a flip of every trit and truncation is already rounding.

In two's complement, negating means inverting and adding one; in balanced ternary you only flip every trit, and the spec's negate() does exactly that, place by place. Cutting the lowest k trits leaves the nearest multiple of 3^k: 8 cut by one trit is 9, 7 is 6. No tie can happen, because the dropped part is always less than half a step, so balanced ternary needs no rounding rule.

Try it

Press flip on 8 and on -121; then cut 13 by one and by two trits and check each result against the nearest multiple.

Open the interactive lesson →
02

Module 2 · Logic with unknown

Kleene's three-valued gates, two gates binary has no twin for, and addition as a pair of tables.

04

Lesson 4 of 27

Three-valued logic

You will learnHow NOT, MIN and MAX extend Boolean logic with an unknown value.

Let -1 be false, +1 true and 0 unknown. AND becomes the minimum, OR the maximum and NOT a flip: Kleene's strong logic. On the four corners of each 3 x 3 table, where no input is unknown, it is exactly Boolean logic; the middle row and column say what a circuit knows when an input does not. The lesson spec writes them as t_not(), t_min() and t_max(), and its tests check the Boolean corners.

Try it

Find the cells of MIN where an unknown input does not change the answer, and the same cells of MAX.

Open the interactive lesson →
05

Lesson 5 of 27

Consensus and any

You will learnTwo gates that only make sense with three values.

CONSENSUS keeps a value both inputs agree on and answers unknown otherwise; ANY takes whichever input is decided and answers unknown only when the two contradict. With two values neither gate has a counterpart, which is part of why a two-input ternary gate has 19683 possible tables. Both are fn bodies of trits.t27, tested on the input pairs that tell them apart.

Try it

Find the inputs where CONSENSUS and ANY give different answers, and name a sensor problem where each would be the right choice.

Open the interactive lesson →
06

Lesson 6 of 27

Sum and carry

You will learnHow the addition of two trits splits into a sum table and a carry table.

Two trits add to something from -2 to +2. Written in balanced ternary that is a sum trit plus three times a carry trit: +1 + +1 = 2 = 3 - 1, carry +1, sum -1. The widget shows both as gates. Counting tables, a two-input ternary gate has 3^9 = 19683 possibilities against 16 in binary. The lesson spec builds XOR from ternary neurons, the hardware side of the same idea.

Try it

Find the two input pairs whose carry is not 0, and check a + b = sum + 3 x carry on each.

Open the interactive lesson →
03

Module 3 · Adding trits

The half adder, the full adder and a carry that ripples left, one place at a time.

07

Lesson 7 of 27

The half adder

You will learnTwo trits in, a sum trit and a carry trit out, for all nine cases.

A half adder is the sum and carry tables wired side by side. The spec computes both from trit_at() of a + b: place 0 is the sum, place 1 the carry. Of the nine input pairs only +1 + +1 and -1 + -1 carry; every other pair fits in one trit. Binary's half adder carries on one case of four, ternary's on two of nine.

Try it

Step through all nine cases in the strip and count how many carry; compare with the four cases of a binary half adder.

Open the interactive lesson →
08

Lesson 8 of 27

The full adder

You will learnWhy three trits still fit one sum trit and one carry trit.

A full adder adds a carry from the place below. Three trits sum to -3..3, and that range is always 3 x carry + sum with both still single trits; the spec's test checks all 27 cases. The lesson spec in the player is a different machine: ternary_full_adder.t27 builds a binary full adder out of ternary neurons, the way the repository's FPGA BitNet work does. Same word, two meanings, both runnable.

Try it

Set all three inputs to +1 and then to -1; read the carry and the sum, and find a case whose carry is 0 though no input is 0.

Open the interactive lesson →
09

Lesson 9 of 27

Ripple carry

You will learnHow a row of full adders adds two numbers, the carry walking left.

Line up full adders, one per place, and feed each carry into the next: a ripple-carry adder. 13 + 1 opens the widget: the ones place makes 2 = 3 - 1, so a carry of +1 walks through three places and +++ becomes +---. The spec's ripple_add() is checked against plain addition on 198 pairs. The lesson spec builds a 2-bit binary ripple adder from the same ternary parts.

Try it

Press play and stop at the column where the carry first turns back to 0; then try 40 + 41.

Open the interactive lesson →
04

Module 4 · Multiplying without a multiplier

Copy, drop or flip: a product by one trit, long multiplication, and a MAC that only adds.

10

Lesson 10 of 27

Times one trit

You will learnWhy multiplying by -1, 0 or +1 is a switch, not a multiplier.

A product by one trit has three cases: +1 copies the number, 0 drops it, -1 flips every trit. The spec's trit_times() is exactly that switch and contains no multiplication. This is why ternary neural networks are cheap in hardware: a weight of -1, 0 or +1 needs a multiplexer and an inverter, not a multiplier.

Try it

Multiply 25 by each trit and compare the tiles; then explain why a weight of 0 costs nothing in hardware.

Open the interactive lesson →
11

Lesson 11 of 27

Long multiplication

You will learnHow n x m becomes rows of copies, zeros and flips.

Each trit of m picks a copy, a zero or a flip of n, shifted one place per row; adding the rows gives the product. 7 x 8: 8 is +0-, so the rows are -7, 0 and 63, which sum to 56. There is no times table to learn, only the three-way switch of the last lesson and an adder. The spec's long_mul() is checked against n x m on 243 pairs.

Try it

Find a pair whose middle row is a copy and whose other rows are zeros; then multiply 13 by 13.

Open the interactive lesson →
12

Lesson 12 of 27

A ternary MAC

You will learnHow a dot product with ternary weights becomes adds, subtracts and skips.

A multiply-accumulate unit adds input times weight, clock after clock. With weights of -1, 0 and +1 each clock is an add, a subtract or nothing: the widget's nine clocks make 4 adds, 2 subtracts and 3 skips and land on -8, with no multiplier. The lesson spec, ternary_mac.t27, is the hardware version: a 27-trit dot product over packed vectors, 2 bits per trit.

Try it

Press weights until the accumulator lands on 0, then on the largest value you can reach.

Open the interactive lesson →
05

Module 5 · Trits in binary memory

Two bits per trit, five trits per byte, and the bits a 27-trit word needs.

13

Lesson 13 of 27

Two bits per trit

You will learnWhat it costs to store a trit in binary the simple way.

Binary memory stores a trit in two bits: -1 as 00, 0 as 01, +1 as 10, the packing this repository's hardware specs use. The code 11 means nothing. A trit carries log2(3) = 1.585 bits of information, so two bits are 79.25% used: a fifth of the memory carries nothing.

Try it

Pick each trit and read its code; say what a decoder should do with 11, and check what the spec's decode2() does.

Open the interactive lesson →
14

Lesson 14 of 27

Five trits in a byte

You will learnHow 3^5 = 243 fits under 2^8 = 256, and what the 13 spare codes mean.

Five trits have 243 combinations and a byte has 256, so five trits fit one byte with 13 codes to spare. The spec packs them as a number in base 3, each trit plus one, and unpacks with division. That uses 99.06% of the byte's information against 79.25% for two bits per trit. Bytes from 243 up are not codes at all.

Try it

Pack +1 +1 +1 +1 +1 and read the byte; then set the byte to 243 and explain what the widget says.

Open the interactive lesson →
15

Lesson 15 of 27

A word of 27 trits

You will learnHow many bits a 27-trit word needs, and how close to full it runs.

k trits need the fewest bits b with 2^b at least 3^k. A 27-trit word, the size of a TRI-27 register, reaches plus or minus 3812798742493 and needs 43 bits. The share of those bits in use climbs in a saw-tooth towards 1 as words grow: wide words waste almost nothing, narrow ones up to a fifth.

Try it

Find the word length above one trit with the worst share, and the one closest to 100%.

Open the interactive lesson →
06

Module 6 · The TRI-27 instruction word

The 32-bit word the Trinity emulator decodes: its fields, its 47 opcodes and its 15-bit immediate.

16

Lesson 16 of 27

The instruction word

You will learnHow the TRI-27 emulator packs an instruction into 32 bits.

The TRI-27 machine computes with trits, but its instructions are 32-bit binary words, decoded by the pinned Trinity emulator. The opcode sits in bits 7..0, the destination register in 12..8, the sources above it; the immediate form gives the top 15 bits to a signed number. The widget calls the spec's encode() and reads every field back with opcode_of(), dst_of() and the rest.

Try it

Encode ADD r1, r2, r3 and LDI r1 with 5; say which bits differ and why the immediate form has a narrower src1.

Open the interactive lesson →
17

Lesson 17 of 27

The opcode map

You will learnWhich of the 256 opcode bytes mean something, and what the rest do.

Of 256 byte values, 47 are TRI-27 opcodes, from NOP and LD through ADD, JMP and HALT to SYSCALL. The other 209 are not errors to the emulator: decode_opcode() reads an unknown byte as NOP, so decoding never fails. The lesson spec, t27a_mnemonics.t27, gives the t27a assembler a strict decoder that refuses those bytes instead.

Try it

Find the opcode bytes of ADD and HALT; then press an unlit byte and say why a strict decoder is safer for an assembler.

Open the interactive lesson →
18

Lesson 18 of 27

The immediate

You will learnHow a 15-bit signed immediate is clamped, stored and read back.

An immediate lives in 15 bits of two's complement: -16384 to 16383. The spec clamps anything outside to the edge rather than wrapping it, so 20000 becomes 16383, and the field round-trips through encode and decode. The lesson spec is the t27a assembler and disassembler, which write and read the same table both ways.

Try it

Try 16383, 16384 and -16385; then find the immediate whose 15 bits are all ones.

Open the interactive lesson →
07

Module 7 · A ternary machine

An ALU built from this course's adders, a three-way jump, and a program you can step.

19

Lesson 19 of 27

A ternary ALU

You will learnHow add, subtract, negate and compare work on 9-trit registers.

The ALU of this widget is built from the course so far: ADD is the ripple adder, SUB adds b with every trit flipped, NEG is the flip alone, CMP answers one trit. Nine-trit registers hold -9841 to 9841, and a result beyond that is flagged as overflow. The lesson spec, tri27_machine.t27, states the TRI-27 machine as the Trinity emulator executes it.

Try it

Subtract 13 from 40 and read the tiles; then make the adder overflow with the smallest pair you can.

Open the interactive lesson →
20

Lesson 20 of 27

A three-way jump

You will learnWhy one ternary compare can branch three ways.

A binary machine branches on a flag: to tell less, equal and greater apart it tests twice. A ternary compare answers with one trit, so one instruction can jump three ways. The widget compares a and b at their first differing trit, lit gold, and takes the matching target. The machine of the next lesson ends its loops with exactly this jump.

Try it

Make the jump take each of the three targets; then find two numbers that differ only in their lowest trit.

Open the interactive lesson →
21

Lesson 21 of 27

Run a program

You will learnHow five instructions and one three-way jump make a loop that ends itself.

The widget's machine has three 9-trit registers and five instructions: SET, ADD, DEC, BR3 and HALT. Sum 1..n sets r1 to n, adds it into r0, decrements, and BR3 jumps back while r1 is positive; at 0 it falls through to HALT. For n = 5 it halts with r0 = 15. The lesson spec describes the .tbin container a TRI-27 program ships in, as the Trinity loader reads it.

Try it

Step the sum program clock by clock for n = 3; then run 7 x n for n = 12 and count the clocks.

Open the interactive lesson →
08

Module 8 · Three answers

Compare at the highest differing trit, find a number in thirds, sort with three-way compares.

22

Lesson 22 of 27

Compare at the top

You will learnWhy balanced-ternary numbers compare at their first differing trit.

In balanced ternary the trits below place i add up to less than half of 3^i, so the highest differing trit decides any comparison. 41 is +---- and 39 is 0+++0: they differ in the top trit, so 41 is greater although its tiles show four minus signs. The spec's compare() reads that trit and is checked against plain less and greater on 714 pairs.

Try it

Find two numbers that first differ in their lowest trit, and two that differ in every trit.

Open the interactive lesson →
23

Lesson 23 of 27

Questions in thirds

You will learnWhy three-answer questions find a number faster, and spell it as they go.

Ask which third of the range a hidden number lies in, and each answer is one of three: low, middle, high. Over the range -121..121 the answers, from the top, are exactly the number's five trits. Among 243 numbers that takes 5 questions; yes-or-no questions need 8. The spec's questions3() and questions2() count both.

Try it

Hide 23 and ask until it is found; then hide -121 and say what every answer was.

Open the interactive lesson →
24

Lesson 24 of 27

Sort with three-way compares

You will learnHow a sort uses compares that also answer equal.

Three compares sort three numbers: the left pair, the right pair, then the left pair again. Each compare answers less, equal or greater in one go, so two equal sevens are settled by a single compare and never swapped. Sorting with ties then needs no extra test.

Try it

Sort 7, -2, 7; then find an order of three different numbers that needs no swap at all.

Open the interactive lesson →
09

Module 9 · Ternary neurons

Weights of -1, 0, +1: one neuron, a detector and a small layer, with no multiplier anywhere.

25

Lesson 25 of 27

One ternary neuron

You will learnHow a neuron with weights -1, 0, +1 computes without multiplying.

A neuron multiplies each input by a weight, adds the products and compares the sum with a threshold. With ternary weights every product is a copy, a zero or a flip, so the sum is adds and subtracts only. The spec's activate() answers +1 at or above the threshold, -1 at or below minus it and 0 between: a neuron that can say not sure.

Try it

Draw a vertical bar on the input and raise the threshold until the neuron stops firing; then press weights until it fires on a horizontal bar.

Open the interactive lesson →
26

Lesson 26 of 27

A bar detector

You will learnWhy a neuron's weights work as a template.

Give the neuron the weights of a vertical bar and its sum counts agreements minus disagreements with them. The vertical bar sums to 9 and fires +1, the inverted bar sums to -9 and fires -1, the horizontal bar and the diagonal sum to 1 and noise to 0. The lesson spec is the same neuron in hardware: a combinational BitNet neuron over one 27-trit chunk.

Try it

Edit the input until the sum is exactly the threshold 5; then find the smallest change to the vertical bar that stops it firing.

Open the interactive lesson →
27

Lesson 27 of 27

A tiny layer

You will learnHow several neurons reading one input describe it with a few trits.

A layer is several neurons that read the same input. Three detectors, vertical, horizontal and diagonal, turn a 3 x 3 picture into three output trits: a vertical bar gives +1, 0, 0. Stack layers and you have a network; the lesson spec is a 4-neuron layer in one combinational module, and the ai-numbers course takes it to a whole network on the board.

Try it

Draw a picture that makes two neurons fire at once; then one that makes all three answer -1.

TRI CLAW

The agent behind t27, in Telegram and on GitHub

TRI CLAW is the project's agent: it writes and checks .t27 specs with you. Three ways to use it.

  • Free, with your own key

    Add your own API key (NVIDIA or z.ai today) and the agent runs on it. Add more keys any time.

    Add a key in Telegram ↗

  • We do it for you

    No keys to keep: join the club in our Telegram bot and the agent runs on ours. The bot shows the price before you pay.

    Join the club in Telegram ↗

  • On GitHub

    TRI CLAW is also a GitHub App, built to check the .t27 specs a pull request changes. It is not open to other repositories yet.

    Read about TRI CLAW ↗
